When solving an exercise at the end of [Chapter 22](../chapters/ch22-dasg-arch-simon-invertible-matrices.qmd) or [Chapter 24](../chapters/ch24-goulden-jackson-moment-shift-fps.qmd), the chapter title itself hands you the governing mathematical structure before you read a single word of the problem statement. In a live contest, **problems arrive completely untagged**. You are presented with a story about subsequence extraction across substring intervals $[l, r]$, semi-local sequence comparison, or occurrence moments in random character streams of length $n \le 10^{18}$, and you must determine on your own whether the transition matrix is invertible in $O(|\Sigma|)$, requires a Segment Tree or Planar Uncrossing Permutation, or collapses via a generating-function shift.

This checkpoint tests **blind diagnostic recognition** across all four chapters of Part VI (`Ch 22`–`Ch 25`). None of the visible problem statements in Section 2 reveal which chapter or technique applies.

::: {.callout-important title="Zero-Spoiler Protocol & Progressive Hints"}
1. **Strict Zero-Spoiler Rule in Visible Statements**: Every problem statement (`CP-VI-01` through `CP-VI-08`) is written in pure contest form without naming the target chapter (`Ch 22`–`Ch 25`) or technique (`DASG`, `Invertible Subsequence Matrix`, `Seaweed Matrix`, `Bit-Parallel LCS`, `Goulden–Jackson`, `Martingale PGF`, `DP套DP`).
2. **Diagnose Before Peeking**: Before opening any dropdown on a problem, write down on scratch paper:
   - Which **Part VI paradigm** (`Ch 22`–`Ch 25`) is triggered by the algebraic domain, constraints, and query geometry;
   - Which **lookalike decoy paradigm** must be ruled out, and why;
   - The **combinatorial word invariant** that collapses the naive exponential, cubic, or $\Theta(n)$ bottleneck.
3. **Four-Stage Progressive Unmasking**:
   - **Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination**: Explains how to identify the governing paradigm and rule out lookalike decoys purely from constraints and query semantics.
   - **Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant**: States the exact algebraic, planar-braid, or generating-function identity needed for the reduction.
   - **Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly**: Outlines the state representation, transition order, and complexity target.
   - **Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution**: Full proof, boundary pitfall audit (`BP-6-01` through `BP-6-08`), and non-standard reference kernel where clarifying.

## 1. Blind Diagnostic Triage Guide & Decoy Elimination

Part VI contest problems frequently disguise themselves behind two classic **Diagnostic Decoy Groups**: (A) range subsequence queries on $S[l..r]$ where four superficially similar recurrences require four completely different data structures, and (B) pattern-occurrence counting / expectation problems where small-$N$ polynomial extraction, huge-$n$ moment shifting, stopping-time martingales, and outer automaton enumeration look nearly identical at first glance.

### 1.1 Decoy Triad A: Range Subsequence Algebra (`Ch 22`) vs. Semi-Local Alignment (`Ch 23`)

Suppose a problem gives a string $S[1..N]$ (or pair $A[1..M], B[1..N]$) and asks $Q$ range queries on $S[l..r]$ (or $B[l..r]$) involving scattered subsequences. Before coding a Segment Tree of matrices, test three diagnostic questions: **(1) What is the semiring?** **(2) What is the determinant $\det M_c$ of the single-character step?** **(3) Are we comparing against an external string $A$ of length $M \gg 1$?**

| Diagnostic Dimension | `Ch 22` Invertible Ring Matrix (`T-4B-03`, $\det M_c \in \mathcal{R}^\times$) | `Ch 22` Non-Invertible Tropical / Gap-2 Matrix (`T-4B-03`, No Inverse) | `Ch 22` Arch Binary Lifting (`T-4B-02`, Universality / `SAS`) | `Ch 23` Tiskin's Seaweed Braid (`T-4B-04`, Semi-Local `LCS` / `LIS`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Governing Semiring & Determinant** | Commutative ring $(\mathcal{R}, +, \times)$ with $\det M_c = 1$ (unweighted / unitriangular) or $\det M_c = \alpha_c \in \mathcal{R}^\times$. | Tropical semiring $(\mathbb{Z}\cup\{\infty\}, \min, +)$ (**no additive inverse**) OR ring DP with buffered overwrite (**$\det M_c = 0$**). | Greedy complete-alphabet partition (`nxt[i][c]`); each arch $A_r$ consumes all $\sigma$ letters once. | Unit-Monge $(\max, +)$ / $(\min, +)$ alignment grid reduced to a $0$-Hecke sticky braid permutation $W[1..N]$. |
| **Why Prefix Inversion Succeeds or Fails** | New state $w'_c = \sum_j w_j$ **includes old $w_c$ with coefficient $+1$**, so $M_c = I + \mathbf{e}_c\sum_{j\ne c}\mathbf{e}_j^T$ has $O(1)$-sparse inverse $M_c^{-1}$. | In $(\min, +)$, $\min(a, b)$ cannot be undone; in gap-2 ($i_{t+1} \ge i_t + 2$), old $w_c$ is overwritten by delayed buffer without $+w_c$, losing rank! | Shortest absent subsequence length equals $\iota(S[l..r]) + 1$; greedy arch endpoints compose associatively via functional jumping. | Alignment paths from top/left to bottom/right uncross at most once (`u > W[j]`), encoding all $\binom{N+1}{2}$ intervals in $N$ integers. |
| **Optimal Query Complexity** | **$O(|\Sigma|)$ or $O(K)$ dot product** $\mathbf{u}_r^T \cdot \mathbf{v}_{l-1}$ with **zero Segment Trees**! | **$O(K^2 \log N)$ Segment Tree** (vector-matrix propagation across $O(\log N)$ nodes) or Divide-and-Conquer. | **$O(\log N)$ binary lifting** on $\text{up}[k][i]$ (`arch_end[i] = max_c nxt[i][c]`). | **$O(\log N)$ 2D dominance count** $\#\{k \in [l, r] \mid -i \le W[k] < l\}$ via Chairman Tree. |
| **Fatal Misdiagnosis** | Building a Segment Tree of $27\times 27$ matrices ($O(Q\sigma^3\log N)$ TLE) when $\det M_c = 1$. | Trying to invert $M_c$ for gap-2 subsequences (`ABC 214F`) or $(\min, +)$ deletion cost (`CF 750E`). | Using forward greedy $\arg\max_c \text{nxt}[u][c]$ to reconstruct the *lex-smallest* absent witness (breaks ties wrong!). | Running $O(MN)$ LCS DP from scratch for each query $[l, r]$, or confusing $W[k] < l$ with $p[i] > r$. |

### 1.2 Decoy Pair B: Bivariate $(t-1)$ vs. $t = 1 + u$ Cluster GFs (`Ch 24`) vs. Martingale PGFs & `DP套DP` (`Ch 25`)

Suppose a problem asks to count strings $W \in \Sigma^n$ (or compute an expectation over $W \in \Sigma^*$) governed by pattern occurrences or an inner dynamic program. Look immediately at **whether the process stops at the first hit ($T_P$)** versus **runs for a fixed length $n$**, and compare **$n$ against the pattern length $|P| = L$**:

| Diagnostic Dimension | `Ch 24` Bivariate $(t-1)$ Exact-$k$ FPS (`T-4A-02`) | `Ch 24` The $t = 1 + u$ Binomial Moment Shift (`T-4A-03`) | `Ch 25` Conway's Casino Martingale PGF (`T-4A-04`) | `Ch 25` 4-Stage `DP套DP` Automaton Compiler (`T-4A-05`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Target Quantity & Regime** | Exact count $[x^N t^k]F(x, t)$ of length-$N$ words with **exactly $k$ occurrences** of $P$, for moderate **$N \le 10^5, L \le 10^5$**. | $K$-th moment $\mathbb{E}[\text{occ}_P(W)^K]$ at **fixed huge length $n \le 10^{18}$** with long pattern **$L \le 10^5$** and small $K \le 20$. | Expected **stopping time** $\mathbb{E}[T_S]$, $\operatorname{Var}(T_S)$, $\mathbb{E}[T_{S,k}]$, or winning probabilities $\pi_i$ in an **unbounded stream**. | Count outer strings $T \in \Sigma^N$ classified by the output of an **inner DP** $f(S, T) = k$ (e.g., $\operatorname{LCS}(S, T) = k$ for $|S| \le 18$). |
| **Governing Algebraic Identity** | Expand around $t = 0$: $[t^k]F(x, t) = \dfrac{x^L D_1(x)^{k-1}}{D_0(x)^{k+1}}$, where $D_0(0) = 1$ and $D_1(x)$ has valuation $d_{\min} = \min\operatorname{Per}(P) \ge 1$. | Expand around **$t = 1$ ($t = 1 + u$)**: $[u^j]F(x, 1+u) = \dfrac{x^L D_1(x)^{j-1}}{(1 - \sigma x)^{j+1}}$, **collapsing the denominator degree from $(j+1)L$ to $j+1$**! | Optional Stopping at $T = \min_i T_{P_i}$ yields the $(m+1)\times(m+1)$ overlap system $\sum_i \pi_i \Phi_{i,j} - \mathbb{P}(P_j)\mathbb{E}[T] = 0$. | Compress inner DP row by relative differences $\Delta_j \in \{0, 1\}$ (`Ch 23` 4-op Allison–Dix bitmask) + BFS / Hopcroft minimization. |
| **Fatal Misdiagnosis** | Calling `poly_ln(D_1)` directly without factoring out $x^{d_{\min}}$ ($D_1(0) = 0$!). | Expanding around $t = 0$ and attempting Bostan–Mori on denominator $D_0(x)^{K+1}$ of degree $KL \approx 10^6$ at $n = 10^{18}$. | Transposing winner $P_i$ and gambler $P_j$ in $\Omega_{P_i, P_j}$, or dividing by $\mathbb{P}(P_j[1..k])$ when zero-probability letters exist. | Unpacking the $K$-bit mask into an array inside the outer DP loop instead of precomputing `trans[mask][c]` in $O(1)$ bitwise steps. |

## 2. Unspoiled Blind Checkpoint Problems (`CP-VI-01` – `CP-VI-08`)

---

### Problem `CP-VI-01` — High-Throughput Substring Subsequence Fingerprinting

You are given a string $S[1..N]$ over the first $\sigma$ lowercase English letters ($1 \le \sigma \le 26$) and $Q$ independent range queries ($1 \le N \le 2 \times 10^5$, $1 \le Q \le 5 \times 10^5$). Each query specifies a substring interval $[l, r]$ ($1 \le l \le r \le N$) and asks for the number of **distinct non-empty subsequences** of the substring $S[l..r]$, modulo $10^9 + 7$.

(Two subsequences drawn from different index tuples inside $[l, r]$ are considered identical if and only if they spell the exact same character string.)

- **Constraints**: $1 \le N \le 2 \times 10^5$, $1 \le Q \le 5 \times 10^5$, $1 \le \sigma \le 26$, Time Limit $1.5\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination**: With $Q = 5 \times 10^5$ and $\sigma = 26$, building a Segment Tree of $(\sigma + 1) \times (\sigma + 1)$ transition matrices (or running Divide-and-Conquer) requires at least $O(Q \sigma^2 \log N) \approx 6 \times 10^9$ operations, which will TLE by a wide margin.
- **Diagnostic Signal**: Write down the standard left-to-right DP state $\mathbf{w} = (w_1, \dots, w_\sigma, w_{\sigma+1})^T$, where $w_a$ counts distinct subsequences ending with character $a \in \{1, \dots, \sigma\}$ and $w_{\sigma+1} = 1$ represents the empty string $\varepsilon$. When character $c = S[i]$ is read, $w'_c = \sum_{j=1}^{\sigma+1} w_j$ and $w'_a = w_a$ ($a \ne c$). Because the old value $w_c$ appears inside $\sum_{j=1}^{\sigma+1} w_j$ with coefficient $+1$, the transition matrix $M_c$ is an **elementary row-addition matrix with determinant $\det(M_c) = 1$**—invertible over every commutative ring!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
Let $P_i = M_{S[i]} M_{S[i-1]} \cdots M_{S[1]}$ ($P_0 = I_{\sigma+1}$). The transition matrix over $S[l..r]$ is $M_{S[r]} \cdots M_{S[l]} = P_r P_{l-1}^{-1}$, so the total number of distinct subsequences of $S[l..r]$ (including $\varepsilon$) is a **1D bilinear dot product**:
$$\operatorname{Ans}(l, r) + 1 = \mathbf{1}^T \bigl(P_r P_{l-1}^{-1}\bigr) \mathbf{e}_{\sigma+1} = \underbrace{\bigl(\mathbf{1}^T P_r\bigr)}_{\mathbf{u}_r^T \in \mathcal{R}^{1 \times (\sigma+1)}} \cdot \underbrace{\bigl(P_{l-1}^{-1} \mathbf{e}_{\sigma+1}\bigr)}_{\mathbf{v}_{l-1} \in \mathcal{R}^{(\sigma+1) \times 1}} = \sum_{k=1}^{\sigma+1} u_r[k] \cdot v_{l-1}[k].$$
Even better, **neither $P_i$ nor $P_i^{-1}$ needs to be stored as a $(\sigma+1)\times(\sigma+1)$ matrix at each index $i$**:

1. Left-multiplying $P_{i-1}$ by $M_c$ ($c = S[i]$) replaces row $c$ of $P_{i-1}$ (which was set at the previous occurrence $p = \operatorname{last}[c]$ to $\mathbf{u}_{p-1}^T$, or $\mathbf{e}_c^T$ if $p = 0$) with the sum of all rows $\mathbf{1}^T P_{i-1} = \mathbf{u}_{i-1}^T$:
   $$\mathbf{u}_i^T = 2 \mathbf{u}_{i-1}^T - \begin{cases} \mathbf{u}_{\operatorname{last}[c]-1}^T & \text{if } \operatorname{last}[c] \ge 1, \\ \mathbf{e}_c^T & \text{if } \operatorname{last}[c] = 0. \end{cases}$$
2. Right-multiplying $P_{i-1}^{-1}$ by $M_c^{-1} = I_{\sigma+1} - \mathbf{e}_c \sum_{k \ne c} \mathbf{e}_k^T$ leaves column $c$ of $P_{i-1}^{-1}$ unchanged and **subtracts column $c$ from every other column $k \ne c$** (including column $\sigma + 1$).
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}
1. Maintain the columns of $P_i^{-1}$ lazily as $\mathbf{c}_k = \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_k + \mathbf{g}$, where $\mathbf{g} \in \mathcal{R}^{\sigma+1}$ is a global offset vector (initially $\mathbf{g} = \mathbf{0}$ and $\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_k = \mathbf{e}_k$).
2. At step $i = 1, \dots, N$ with $c = S[i]$:
   - Compute $\mathbf{u}_i^T$ in $O(\sigma)$ time using the two-term recurrence above, then set $\operatorname{last}[c] = i$.
   - Read column $c$ of $P_{i-1}^{-1}$ as $\mathbf{w} = \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_c + \mathbf{g}$; subtract $\mathbf{w}$ from all columns via $\mathbf{g} \leftarrow \mathbf{g} - \mathbf{w}$ and restore column $c$ via $\tilde{\mathbf{c}}_c \leftarrow \tilde{\mathbf{c}}_c + \mathbf{w}$.
   - Record $\mathbf{v}_i = \mathbf{c}_{\sigma+1}^{(i)} = \mathbf{e}_{\sigma+1} + \mathbf{g}$ in $O(\sigma)$ time.
3. Answer each query $[l, r]$ in $O(\sigma)$ time by computing $\bigl(\sum_{k=1}^{\sigma+1} u_r[k] v_{l-1}[k] - 1\bigr) \bmod (10^9 + 7)$.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-VI-01"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 22](../chapters/ch22-dasg-arch-simon-invertible-matrices.qmd) (`T-4B-03`: Elementary Subsequence Matrix Invertibility $\det M_c = 1$ & Matrix-Free $O((N+Q)|\Sigma|)$ Bilinear Dot Product · Decoy Triad A Part 1)**.
- **Proof of Matrix-Free Forward & Inverse Vector Updates**:
  For $c \in \{1, \dots, \sigma\}$, write $M_c = I_{\sigma+1} + \mathbf{e}_c \sum_{j \ne c} \mathbf{e}_j^T$. Since $\mathbf{e}_j^T \mathbf{e}_c = 0$ for all $j \ne c$, the nilpotent rank-1 perturbation $N_c = \mathbf{e}_c \sum_{j \ne c} \mathbf{e}_j^T$ satisfies $N_c^2 = 0$, proving $(I_{\sigma+1} + N_c)(I_{\sigma+1} - N_c) = I_{\sigma+1}$ over any commutative ring $\mathcal{R}$.
  In the forward product $P_i = M_c P_{i-1}$, only row $c$ of $P_{i-1}$ is modified, becoming $\sum_{r=1}^{\sigma+1} \mathbf{e}_r^T P_{i-1} = \mathbf{1}^T P_{i-1} = \mathbf{u}_{i-1}^T$. Because row $c$ remained untouched between $p = \operatorname{last}[c]$ and $i - 1$, its value in $P_{i-1}$ equals $\mathbf{u}_{p-1}^T$ (or row $c$ of $P_0 = I_{\sigma+1}$, namely $\mathbf{e}_c^T$, when $p = 0$). Adding the new row $c$ and subtracting the old row $c$ yields $\mathbf{u}_i^T = \mathbf{u}_{i-1}^T + \mathbf{u}_{i-1}^T - \text{old\_row}_c = 2\mathbf{u}_{i-1}^T - \text{old\_row}_c$.
- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-6-01`)**:
  - **Subtracting $\mathbf{0}^T$ Instead of $\mathbf{e}_c^T$ on First Occurrence ($\operatorname{last}[c] = 0$)**: Before character $c$ ever appears in $S$, row $c$ of $P_{i-1}$ is **not** zero—it is the $c$-th row of the identity matrix $P_0 = I_{\sigma+1}$, which has a $1$ in column $c$! Failing to subtract $\mathbf{e}_c^T$ when $\operatorname{last}[c] = 0$ corrupts column $c$ of $\mathbf{u}_i^T$ for the entire remainder of the string.

```cpp
// Matrix-Free O((N + Q) * sigma) Range Distinct Subsequence Engine
int u[N + 1][27], v[N + 1][27], c_tilde[27][27], g[27], last_pos[27];
for (int k = 0; k <= 26; ++k) {
    u[0][k] = 1;
    v[0][k] = (k == 26 ? 1 : 0);
    c_tilde[k][k] = 1;
}
for (int i = 1; i <= n; ++i) {
    int c = S[i - 1] - 'a';
    int p = last_pos[c];
    for (int k = 0; k <= 26; ++k) {
        int old_row = (p == 0) ? (k == c ? 1 : 0) : u[p - 1][k];
        u[i][k] = (2LL * u[i - 1][k] - old_row + MOD) % MOD;
    }
    last_pos[c] = i;
    for (int r = 0; r <= 26; ++r) {
        int w_r = (c_tilde[c][r] + g[r]) % MOD;
        g[r] = (g[r] - w_r + MOD) % MOD;
        c_tilde[c][r] = (c_tilde[c][r] + w_r) % MOD;
        v[i][r] = (g[r] + (r == 26 ? 1 : 0)) % MOD;
    }
}
```

- **Complexity**: $O((N + Q)\sigma)$ time and $O(N\sigma)$ space.

### Problem `CP-VI-02` — Substring Protocol Sanitization

You are given a digit string $S[1..N] \in \{\texttt{'0'}, \dots, \texttt{'9'}\}^N$ and $Q$ range queries ($1 \le N, Q \le 2 \times 10^5$). Each query specifies a substring $S[l..r]$ ($1 \le l \le r \le N$) and asks for the **minimum number of characters that must be deleted** from $S[l..r]$ so that the remaining string:

1. Contains $\texttt{"2017"}$ as a subsequence, **and**
2. Does **not** contain $\texttt{"2016"}$ as a subsequence.

If it is impossible to satisfy both conditions simultaneously for $S[l..r]$, output `-1`.

- **Constraints**: $1 \le N, Q \le 2 \times 10^5$, Time Limit $3.0\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination (`CP-VI-02` vs. `CP-VI-01`)**: Just like `CP-VI-01`, we have a static string $S[1..N]$ and $Q = 2 \times 10^5$ range subsequence queries on $S[l..r]$! Why can't we use prefix matrix inversion $P_r P_{l-1}^{-1}$ here? Because the DP asks for a **minimum deletion cost** over the **tropical semiring $(\mathbb{Z} \cup \{\infty\}, \min, +)$**, and $\min(a, b)$ has **no additive inverse**! Once two path costs merge via $\min$, information about the larger branch is permanently erased.
- **Diagnostic Signal**: Because prefix inversion is algebraically impossible over $(\min, +)$, we must maintain the $5 \times 5$ tropical transition matrices in a **Segment Tree** over $[1, N]$. Moreover, to make queries fast, never multiply two $5 \times 5$ matrices during a query (`O(5^3 log N)`); instead, propagate a $1 \times 5$ state vector left-to-right across the $O(\log N)$ canonical Segment Tree nodes in **$O(5^2 \log N)$** time!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
Track the longest prefix of $\texttt{"2017"}$ matched so far as a 5-state DFA:
$$\mathcal{Q} = \bigl\{0: \varepsilon,\; 1: \texttt{"2"},\; 2: \texttt{"20"},\; 3: \texttt{"201"},\; 4: \texttt{"2017"}\bigr\}.$$
For a single character $c = S[i]$, define the $5 \times 5$ upper-triangular tropical matrix $T_c$ (where $(A \otimes B)_{u, w} = \min_{u \le v \le w} (A_{u, v} + B_{v, w})$), initialized with $T_c[u][u] = 0$ for all $u \in \{0..4\}$ and $+\infty$ elsewhere:

- If $c = \texttt{'2'}$: staying at state $0$ requires deleting $\texttt{'2'}$ ($T_{\texttt{'2'}}[0][0] = 1$), or advancing to state $1$ at cost $0$ ($T_{\texttt{'2'}}[0][1] = 0$).
- If $c = \texttt{'0'}$: $T_{\texttt{'0'}}[1][1] = 1$ (delete $\texttt{'0'}$) and $T_{\texttt{'0'}}[1][2] = 0$ (advance to $\texttt{"20"}$).
- If $c = \texttt{'1'}$: $T_{\texttt{'1'}}[2][2] = 1$ (delete $\texttt{'1'}$) and $T_{\texttt{'1'}}[2][3] = 0$ (advance to $\texttt{"201"}$).
- If $c = \texttt{'7'}$: $T_{\texttt{'7'}}[3][3] = 1$ (delete $\texttt{'7'}$) and $T_{\texttt{'7'}}[3][4] = 0$ (advance to $\texttt{"2017"}$).
- If $c = \texttt{'6'}$: any $\texttt{'6'}$ arriving when we have already matched $\texttt{"201"}$ (state $3$ **or** state $4$!) would complete $\texttt{"2016"}$, so it **must be deleted**:
  $$T_{\texttt{'6'}}[3][3] = 1 \qquad \text{and} \qquad T_{\texttt{'6'}}[4][4] = 1!$$
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}
1. Build a Segment Tree over $1 \le i \le N$ where each node stores the $5 \times 5$ upper-triangular tropical product (`min-plus` over $0 \le u \le v \le w \le 4$, which takes only $\binom{5+2}{3} = 35$ operations per merge instead of $5^3 = 125$!).
2. For each query $[l, r]$:
   - Initialize the $1 \times 5$ row vector $\mathbf{dp} = (0, \infty, \infty, \infty, \infty)$.
   - Traverse the $O(\log N)$ canonical Segment Tree intervals covering $[l, r]$ from left to right, updating $\mathbf{dp}'[w] = \min_{0 \le u \le w} (\mathbf{dp}[u] + M_{\text{node}}[u][w])$ in $\binom{5+1}{2} = 15$ operations per node.
   - Output $\mathbf{dp}[4]$ (or `-1` if $\mathbf{dp}[4] \ge \infty$).
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-VI-02"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 22](../chapters/ch22-dasg-arch-simon-invertible-matrices.qmd) (`T-4B-03` Non-Invertible Counterexample: `CF 750E — New Year and Old Subsequence` · Decoy Triad A Part 2 — Tropical $(\min, +)$ Subsequence Automaton Matrices on a Segment Tree)**.
- **Why State $4$ ($\texttt{"2017"}$) Must Also Delete $\texttt{'6'}$**:
  Once the subsequence $\texttt{"2017"}$ has been formed (reaching state $4$), the prefix $\texttt{"201"}$ is *still* present in the kept characters! If a subsequent $\texttt{'6'}$ is kept while in state $4$, it pairs with that earlier $\texttt{"201"}$ to form the forbidden subsequence $\texttt{"2016"}$. Therefore, both $T_{\texttt{'6'}}[3][3] = 1$ and $T_{\texttt{'6'}}[4][4] = 1$ are mandatory.
- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-6-02`)**:
  - **Forgetting $T_{\texttt{'6'}}[4][4] = 1$**: Setting only $T_{\texttt{'6'}}[3][3] = 1$ allows strings like $\texttt{"20176"}$ to keep the trailing $\texttt{'6'}$ at cost $0$, falsely containing $\texttt{"2016"}$.
  - **Full $5^3$ Matrix Merges During Queries**: Exploiting upper-triangularity ($u \le v \le w$) during `build` ($35$ ops) and propagating a $1 \times 5$ vector during `query` ($15$ ops) speeds up queries by nearly $10\times$.
- **Complexity**: $O(K^3 N + Q K^2 \log N)$ time ($K = 5$) and $O(K^2 N)$ space.
::::

### Problem `CP-VI-03` — Substring Missing-Codeword Oracle

You are given a string $S[1..N]$ over the first $\sigma$ lowercase English letters ($2 \le \sigma \le 26$) and $Q$ online queries ($1 \le N, Q \le 2 \times 10^5$). Each query specifies a substring $S[l..r]$ ($1 \le l \le r \le N$) and asks you to output two values:

1. The **minimum possible length** $L$ of a non-empty string $W \in \Sigma^+$ that does **not** occur as a subsequence of $S[l..r]$;
2. Among all absent strings of that minimum length $L$ for $S[l..r]$, the **first character** $W[1]$ of the **lexicographically smallest** such absent string $W$ (and explain how to reconstruct the entire witness $W[1..L]$ if $\sum L \le 10^6$).

- **Constraints**: $1 \le N, Q \le 2 \times 10^5$, $2 \le \sigma \le 26$, Time Limit $1.5\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination**: Running the backward shortest-path DP $d[i] = 1 + \min_{c \in \Sigma} d[\text{nxt}[i][c]]$ (`ARC 081 E`) from $r$ down to $l - 1$ takes $O((r - l)\sigma)$ per query, which is $\Theta(N Q \sigma)$ in the worst case.
- **Diagnostic Signal**: By **Hébrard's Arch Factorization (`Ch 22` Theorem 22.2)**, a substring $S[l..r]$ contains all $\sigma^k$ strings of length $k$ as subsequences if and only if $S[l..r]$ can be greedily partitioned from left to right into $k$ disjoint $1$-universal **arches** $A_1 A_2 \dots A_k$, where each arch is a minimal contiguous block containing all $\sigma$ letters of $\Sigma$! Because the end of the first arch starting after index $u$ is deterministically $\operatorname{arch\_end}[u] = \max_{c \in \Sigma} \operatorname{nxt}[u][c]$, we can jump across arches using **binary lifting** in $O(\log N)$ time per query!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
For each index $u \in \{0, 1, \dots, N\}$, let $\operatorname{nxt}[u][c] = \min\{j \in [u+1, N] \mid S[j] = c\}$ (with $\min\emptyset = N + 1$), and define the single-arch jump pointer:
$$\operatorname{up}[0][u] = \max_{c \in \Sigma} \operatorname{nxt}[u][c], \qquad \operatorname{up}[b][u] = \operatorname{up}[b-1]\bigl[\operatorname{up}[b-1][u]\bigr].$$
For any query $[l, r]$:

1. Starting from $u_0 = l - 1$, binary lift to find the maximum number of complete arches $k = \iota(S[l..r])$ whose endpoint $u_k = \operatorname{up}^{(k)}[l - 1]$ satisfies $u_k \le r$. Then the Shortest Absent Subsequence of $S[l..r]$ has length **$L = k + 1$**!
2. How do we find the **lexicographically smallest** first character $W[1] = c$ of a length-$(k+1)$ absent subsequence without falling into the forward-greedy trap?
   Choosing $W[1] = c$ jumps from $l - 1$ to $v = \operatorname{nxt}[l - 1][c]$. The suffix $S[v+1..r]$ has a missing subsequence of length $k$ **if and only if** $S[v+1..r]$ contains **at most $k - 1$ complete arches**—which means the $k$-th arch starting after $v$ ends strictly past $r$:
   $$\operatorname{up}^{(k)}[v] > r!$$
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}
1. Sweep $i = N$ down to $0$ to build `nxt[i][0..sigma-1]` and `up[0][i] = max_c nxt[i][c]` in $O(N\sigma)$ time.
2. Build the binary-lifting table `up[b][i]` for $1 \le b \le \lfloor \log_2 N \rfloor$ in $O(N \log N)$ time.
3. For each query $[l, r]$:
   - Binary lift from $u = l - 1$ to find $\iota = k$ (the number of jumps with $\operatorname{up}[b][u] \le r$), so $L = k + 1$.
   - If $k = 0$, $W[1]$ is simply the smallest $c \in \Sigma$ with $\operatorname{nxt}[l - 1][c] > r$.
   - If $k \ge 1$, test $c = 0, 1, \dots, \sigma - 1$ in increasing order and pick the first $c$ whose $k$-arch jump from $v = \operatorname{nxt}[l - 1][c]$ satisfies $\operatorname{up}^{(k)}[v] > r$ (or use monotonicity of $v \mapsto \operatorname{up}^{(k)}[v]$ to binary-search the minimum threshold $v_{\min}$ with $\operatorname{up}^{(k)}[v_{\min}] > r$ and pick the smallest $c$ with $\operatorname{nxt}[l-1][c] \ge v_{\min}$).
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-VI-03"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 22](../chapters/ch22-dasg-arch-simon-invertible-matrices.qmd) (`T-4B-02`: Hébrard's Arch Factorization & $O(\log N)$ Range Shortest Absent Subsequence via Binary Lifting)**.
- **Why Monotonicity of $\operatorname{up}[0][v]$ Gives Fast Lex-Smallest Reconstruction**:
  Because $\operatorname{nxt}[v][c] \le \operatorname{nxt}[v'][c]$ whenever $v \le v'$, the arch jump function $v \mapsto \operatorname{up}[0][v]$ is monotonically non-decreasing, and so is its $k$-fold composition $\operatorname{up}^{(k)}[v]$.
  Suppose $S[l..r]$ has universality index $k \ge 1$ (so $\operatorname{up}^{(k)}[l-1] \le r < \operatorname{up}^{(k+1)}[l-1]$). A first character $c \in \Sigma$ can start a Shortest Absent Subsequence of length $k + 1$ in $S[l..r]$ iff after matching $c$ at $v = \operatorname{nxt}[l-1][c]$, the remaining substring $S[v+1..r]$ is **not** $k$-universal—that is, the $k$-th arch starting after $v$ exceeds $r$:
  $$\operatorname{up}^{(k)}[v] > r.$$
  Iterating this step $L = k + 1$ times (replacing $l - 1 \leftarrow \operatorname{nxt}[l-1][c]$ and $k \leftarrow k - 1$) reconstructs the entire lexicographically smallest witness $W[1..L]$.
- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-6-03`)**:
  - **The Forward-Greedy Tie-Breaking Trap (`ARC 081 E`)**: Picking $c = \arg\max_{c} \operatorname{nxt}[l-1][c]$ (the last character of the first arch) always produces a valid absent subsequence of length $k + 1$, **but not the lexicographically smallest one**! Any character $c$ whose first occurrence $v = \operatorname{nxt}[l-1][c]$ pushes the $k$-th subsequent arch past $r$ ($\operatorname{up}^{(k)}[v] > r$) also achieves length $k + 1$, and we must pick the smallest such letter $c$.
- **Complexity**: $O(N(\sigma + \log N))$ preprocessing and $O(\sigma \log N)$ per query.
::::

### Problem `CP-VI-04` — All-Pairs Prefix–Substring Alignment Oracle

You are given two strings $A[1..M]$ and $B[1..N]$ ($1 \le M, N \le 3000$) and $Q$ online alignment queries ($1 \le Q \le 3 \times 10^5$). Each query specifies a prefix $A[1..i]$ of $A$ ($1 \le i \le M$) and a contiguous substring $B[l..r]$ of $B$ ($1 \le l \le r \le N$), and asks for the maximum length of a string $W$ that occurs simultaneously as a subsequence of $A[1..i]$ and as a subsequence of $B[l..r]$.

- **Constraints**: $1 \le M, N \le 3000$, $1 \le Q \le 3 \times 10^5$, Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination (`Ch 23` vs. `Ch 22`)**: Here the target is the **Longest Common Subsequence** $\operatorname{LCS}(A[1..i], B[l..r])$ of $A[1..i]$ (up to $M = 3000$ characters) and $B[l..r]$. Neither invertible subsequence matrices (`Ch 22`, which count distinct subsequences of a single string) nor a $3000 \times 3000$ tropical Segment Tree can answer $3 \times 10^5$ queries in time.
- **Diagnostic Signal**: This is a **Semi-Local LCS (`Ch 23` `T-4B-04`: Tiskin's Seaweed Matrix)** problem! For a fixed string $A[1..i]$ against all substrings $B[l..r]$, a single Seaweed permutation $W^{(i)}[1..N]$ of length $N$ encodes all $\binom{N+1}{2}$ interval answers via $\operatorname{LCS}(A[1..i], B[l..r]) = \#\{k \in [l, r] \mid W^{(i)}[k] < l\}$. Moreover, when the $O(MN)$ Seaweed Comb sweeps rows $x = 1, 2, \dots, M$ of $A$, the wire array in memory after row $i$ is **literally $W^{(i)}[1..N]$**!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
In Tiskin's Seaweed Comb on $A[1..M] \times B[1..N]$, initialize the top entrance wires at columns $j = 1, \dots, N$ to $W[j] = j$.
In row $x = 1, 2, \dots, M$, introduce a left-wall wire $u = -x < 0$ and sweep $j = 1, \dots, N$ with the sticky uncrossing rule:
$$\text{if } \bigl(A[x] == B[j] \;\text{ or }\; u > W[j]\bigr) \quad \operatorname{swap}(u, W[j]);$$
Let $W^{(i)}[1..N]$ be the bottom-wire array **immediately after finishing row $i$**, and let $R[1..M]$ be the right-wall exit array at the end of row $M$. Then:

1. **Arbitrary 3-Parameter Prefix–Substring Queries $(i, l, r)$**:
   $$\boxed{\operatorname{LCS}\bigl(A[1..i],\, B[l..r]\bigr) = \#\Bigl\{\, k \in [l, r] \;\Big|\; W^{(i)}[k] < l \,\Bigr\}.}$$
2. **Signed-Port Single-Pass Specializations ($l = 1$ or $r = N$ or 1-Match-Per-Row)**:
   Because row $x$ enters with negative port label $-x \in \{-M, \dots, -1\}$, for Suffix–Prefix queries ($l = 1$) or Prefix–Suffix queries ($r = N$) or sparse 1-match-per-row grids (such as Range LIS where $A = (1..N)$), a **single** final Seaweed array $W^{(M)}[1..N]$ answers queries via initial-rank thresholding $-i \le W[k] < l$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}
1. Run the 8-line Seaweed Comb across rows $i = 1, \dots, M$ and columns $j = 1, \dots, N$ in $O(MN)$ time.
2. For $M, N \le 3000$:
   - **Offline / Row-Sweep Mode ($O(N)$ space)**: Bucket queries by $i \in \{1, \dots, M\}$; at the end of row $i$, insert the points $(k, W^{(i)}[k])$ into a Fenwick Tree (or update only the columns $j$ where `swap(u, W[j])` occurred in row $i$) to answer all queries for row $i$ in $O(\log N)$ time.
   - **Online Mode ($O(MN)$ space)**: Store `W_snap[i][k]` (or a persistent Fenwick / Chairman Tree over the swapped columns of row $i$) and count $\#\{k \in [l, r] \mid W^{(i)}[k] < l\}$ in $O(\log N)$ time per query.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-VI-04"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 23](../chapters/ch23-bit-parallel-lcs-seaweed-matrices.qmd) (`T-4B-04`: Tiskin's Seaweed Matrix & Semi-Local LCS Dominance · Decoy Triad A Part 3)**.
- **Proof of the Seaweed Dominance Identity $\operatorname{LCS}(A[1..i], B[l..r]) = \#\{k \in [l, r] \mid W^{(i)}[k] < l\}$**:
  By `Ch 23` Theorem 23.3 (Planar Alignment Uncrossing), the cross-difference $\Delta(l, r) = L(l-1, r) - L(l, r) - L(l-1, r-1) + L(l, r-1) \in \{0, 1\}$ of $L(l, r) = \operatorname{LCS}(A[1..i], B[l+1..r])$ is a sub-permutation matrix whose $1$-entries $(l, k)$ mark the exact bottom column $k$ where the top wire entering at column $l$ exits after $i$ rows ($W^{(i)}[k] = l$).
  Summing $\Delta$ over the complement triangle inside $[l, r]$ shows that $(r - l + 1) - \operatorname{LCS}(A[1..i], B[l..r])$ equals the number of top wires entering in $[l, r]$ that exit at a bottom column $k \in [l, r]$ (i.e., $\#\{k \in [l, r] \mid W^{(i)}[k] \ge l\}$). Subtracting from $r - l + 1$ yields $\#\{k \in [l, r] \mid W^{(i)}[k] < l\}$.
- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-6-04`)**:
  - **Confusing Top-to-Bottom $p[t] > r$ with Bottom-to-Top $W[k] < l$**: If $p[t]$ is the bottom exit column of top wire $t \in [l, r]$, the condition is $p[t] > r$ (strictly greater). If $W[k]$ is the initial entrance rank of the wire exiting at bottom column $k \in [l, r]$, the condition is $W[k] < l$ (strictly less, which includes negative left-border rowports $-x < 0 < l$).

```cpp
// O(M * N) Seaweed Comb with Row Snapshots for Prefix-Substring LCS(A[1..i], B[l..r])
vector<int> W(N + 1);
for (int j = 1; j <= N; ++j) W[j] = j;
for (int i = 1; i <= M; ++i) {
    int u = -i;
    for (int j = 1; j <= N; ++j) {
        if (A[i - 1] == B[j - 1] || u > W[j]) {
            std::swap(u, W[j]);
        }
    }
    // W[1..N] is now W^{(i)}[1..N]: LCS(A[1..i], B[l..r]) = #{k in [l, r] : W[k] < l}
    record_row_snapshot(i, W);
}
```

- **Complexity**: $O(MN + Q \log N)$ time and $O(MN)$ space.
::::

### Problem `CP-VI-05` — Exact Pattern Multiplicity Spectrum

You are given an alphabet $\Sigma$ of size $\sigma$ ($2 \le \sigma \le 26$), a pattern string $P[1..L]$ of length $L$ ($1 \le L \le 5 \times 10^4$), a text length $N$ ($L \le N \le 10^5$), and a target occurrence count $k$ ($1 \le k \le \lfloor N / L \rfloor$).

Count how many strings $W \in \Sigma^N$ of length $N$ contain **exactly $k$ (possibly overlapping) occurrences** of $P$ as a contiguous substring, modulo $998244353$.

- **Constraints**: $1 \le L \le 5 \times 10^4$, $L \le N \le 10^5$, $1 \le k \le \lfloor N / L \rfloor$, $2 \le \sigma \le 26$, Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination (`CP-VI-05` vs. `CP-VI-06`)**: With $L = 5 \times 10^4$ and $N = 10^5$, running KMP DP over `(index i, kmp_state u, count c)` takes $\Theta(N L k)$ time, which is $\ge 5 \times 10^9$ operations even for $k = 1$. On the other hand, $N \le 10^5$ is moderate (unlike `CP-VI-06` where $n = 10^{18}$), and we want the **exact coefficient $[x^N t^k]F(x, t)$ around $t = 0$** rather than a low-order factorial moment around $t = 1$.
- **Diagnostic Signal**: By the **Bivariate $(t-1)$ Cluster Generating Function (`Ch 24` `T-4A-02`)**, marking any subset of occurrences of $P$ with weight $(t - 1)$ collapses all $L$ internal KMP states into a single rational bivariate OGF $F(x, t)$ expressed solely in terms of the autocorrelation polynomial $C_P(x) = \sum_{b \in \operatorname{Border}^+(P)} x^{L - b}$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
Let $C_P(x) = 1 + \sum_{b \in \operatorname{Border}(P)} x^{L - b}$ be the autocorrelation polynomial of $P$ (where the improper border $b = L$ contributes $x^0 = 1$). Define the two degree-$L$ polynomials:
$$D_0(x) = (1 - \sigma x) C_P(x) + x^L, \qquad D_1(x) = (1 - \sigma x)\bigl(C_P(x) - 1\bigr) + x^L = D_0(x) - (1 - \sigma x).$$
Then the bivariate generating function $F(x, t) = \sum_{W \in \Sigma^*} x^{|W|} t^{\operatorname{occ}_P(W)}$ equals $\dfrac{C_P(x) - t(C_P(x) - 1)}{D_0(x) - t D_1(x)}$, and for every $k \ge 1$, the OGF of words with **exactly $k$ occurrences** of $P$ is:
$$\boxed{F_k(x) = [t^k] F(x, t) = \frac{x^L \, D_1(x)^{k-1}}{D_0(x)^{k+1}}!}$$
*Combinatorial 3-piece reading*: $\dfrac{x^L}{D_0(x)}$ generates the prefix ending at the $1$st occurrence of $P$; each of the $k - 1$ factors $\dfrac{D_1(x)}{D_0(x)}$ advances from the $r$-th occurrence of $P$ to the $(r+1)$-th occurrence (either overlapping along a proper border in $C_P(x) - 1$ or restarting after an avoiding bridge); and $\dfrac{1}{D_0(x)}$ generates the $P$-avoiding suffix after the $k$-th occurrence!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}
1. Compute the KMP prefix array $\pi[1..L]$ of $P$ and construct $C_P(x)$ by setting bit/coefficient $x^{L - b}$ for $b = L, \pi[L], \pi[\pi[L]], \dots > 0$.
2. Form $D_0(x)$ and $D_1(x)$ modulo $x^{N - L + 1}$.
3. **Critical Valuation Adjustment Before Calling `poly_ln`**:
   - Observe that $D_0(0) = 1$, so $D_0(x)^{-(k+1)} = \exp\bigl(-(k+1)\ln D_0(x)\bigr)$ can be computed directly via FPS $\ln/\exp$.
   - However, **$D_1(0) = 0$**! The lowest nonzero term of $D_1(x)$ has degree $d_{\min} = L - \pi[L] = \min\operatorname{Per}(P) \ge 1$!
   - If $(k - 1) d_{\min} > N - L$, output `0` immediately (not enough room for $k$ occurrences even at maximum overlap!).
   - Otherwise, factor $D_1(x) = c_0 x^{d_{\min}} \widetilde{D}_1(x)$ with $\widetilde{D}_1(0) = 1$, compute $\widetilde{D}_1(x)^{k-1} D_0(x)^{-(k+1)} \bmod x^{N - L - (k-1)d_{\min} + 1}$ via FPS $\ln/\exp$ in $O(N \log N)$ time, and multiply by $c_0^{k-1}$.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-VI-05"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 24](../chapters/ch24-goulden-jackson-moment-shift-fps.qmd) (`T-4A-02`: Bivariate $(t-1)$ Exact $k$-Occurrence FPS & Valuation Shift $x^{d_{\min}}$ · Decoy Pair B Part 1)**.
- **Algebraic Proof of $[t^k]F(x, t) = \frac{x^L D_1(x)^{k-1}}{D_0(x)^{k+1}}$**:
  In the cluster expansion $F(x, t) = \bigl(1 - \sigma x - C_1(x, t)\bigr)^{-1}$ with $C_1(x, t) = \frac{(t-1)x^L}{1 - (t-1)(C_P(x)-1)}$, clearing the fraction gives $F(x, t) = \frac{C_P(x) - t(C_P(x) - 1)}{D_0(x) - t D_1(x)}$. Expanding $\frac{1}{D_0(x) - t D_1(x)} = \sum_{k \ge 0} t^k \frac{D_1(x)^k}{D_0(x)^{k+1}}$, the coefficient of $t^k$ ($k \ge 1$) is:
  $$[t^k]F(x, t) = \frac{C_P(x) D_1(x)^k - (C_P(x) - 1) D_0(x) D_1(x)^{k-1}}{D_0(x)^{k+1}} = \frac{\bigl(C_P(x) D_1(x) - (C_P(x) - 1) D_0(x)\bigr) D_1(x)^{k-1}}{D_0(x)^{k+1}}.$$
  Substituting $D_1(x) = D_0(x) - (1 - \sigma x)$ and $D_0(x) = (1 - \sigma x)C_P(x) + x^L$ simplifies the bracketed numerator to $C_P(x) D_0(x) - (1 - \sigma x)C_P(x) - C_P(x) D_0(x) + D_0(x) = D_0(x) - (1 - \sigma x)C_P(x) = x^L$!
- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-6-05`)**:
  - **Calling `poly_ln(D_1)` Directly When $D_1(0) = 0$**: Because $C_P(0) = 1$, $D_1(0) = 1 \cdot (1 - 1) + 0 = 0$. The first nonzero term of $D_1(x) = (1 - \sigma x)(C_P(x) - 1) + x^L$ occurs at degree $d_{\min} = L - \pi[L] \ge 1$ with coefficient $1$. Always divide $D_1(x)$ by $x^{d_{\min}}$ (and normalize its leading coefficient if $d_{\min} = 1$ and $x^1$ combines with $-\sigma x^1$) before invoking `poly_ln`.
- **Complexity**: $O(L + N \log N)$ time and $O(N)$ space.
::::

### Problem `CP-VI-06` — Huge-Stream Third-Moment Anomaly

A uniform random generator emits a string $W \in \Sigma^n$ of length $n$ ($1 \le n \le 10^{18}$) over an alphabet $\Sigma$ of size $\sigma$ ($2 \le \sigma < 998244353$). You are given a fixed pattern $P[1..L]$ of length $L$ ($1 \le L \le 10^5$). Let $\operatorname{occ}_P(W)$ denote the total number of (possibly overlapping) occurrences of $P$ in $W$.

Compute the expected cube of the number of occurrences:
$$\mathbb{E}\bigl[\operatorname{occ}_P(W)^3\bigr] = \frac{1}{\sigma^n} \sum_{W \in \Sigma^n} \operatorname{occ}_P(W)^3 \pmod{998244353}.$$

- **Constraints**: $1 \le n \le 10^{18}$, $1 \le L \le 10^5$, $2 \le \sigma < 998244353$, Time Limit $2.0\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination (`CP-VI-06` vs. `CP-VI-05`)**: If you try to use `CP-VI-05`'s expansion around $t = 0$, $[t^k]F(x, t)$ has denominator $D_0(x)^{k+1}$ of degree $(k+1)L \approx 4 \times 10^5$, and at $n = 10^{18}$, extracting $[x^n]$ via Bostan–Mori would take $O(L \log L \log n) \approx 60$ NTTs of size $10^6$ (or fails completely if you try to sum over $k \le n/L$!).
- **Diagnostic Signal**: Instead of expanding $F(x, t)$ around $t = 0$ (which counts exact occurrences $[t^k]$), **substitute $t = 1 + u$ and expand around $t = 1$ ($u = 0$)**! Why does $t = 1 + u$ work miracles at $n = 10^{18}$? Because at $u = 0$ ($t = 1$), $F(x, 1) = \sum_{W \in \Sigma^*} x^{|W|} = \frac{1}{1 - \sigma x}$—all pattern-dependent terms in the denominator **vanish at $u = 0$**, collapsing the denominator of $[u^j]F(x, 1 + u)$ from $D_0(x)^{j+1}$ (degree $(j+1)L$) to **$(1 - \sigma x)^{j+1}$ (degree $j + 1 \le 4$)**!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
Substituting $t = 1 + u$ (so $t - 1 = u$) into the cluster OGF $F(x, t) = \dfrac{1}{1 - \sigma x - \frac{(t-1)x^L}{1 - (t-1)(C_P(x)-1)}}$ yields:
$$F(x, 1 + u) = \sum_{j \ge 0} u^j \sum_{W \in \Sigma^*} \binom{\operatorname{occ}_P(W)}{j} x^{|W|} = \frac{1}{1 - \sigma x} + \sum_{j \ge 1} u^j \, \frac{x^L \, D_1(x)^{j-1}}{(1 - \sigma x)^{j+1}},$$
where $D_1(x) = (1 - \sigma x)\bigl(C_P(x) - 1\bigr) + x^L$ is a **polynomial of degree at most $L$**!
Look at the expression for $B_j(n) = \sum_{W \in \Sigma^n} \binom{\operatorname{occ}_P(W)}{j}$ for $j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$:
$$\boxed{B_j(n) = [x^n] \frac{x^L \, D_1(x)^{j-1}}{(1 - \sigma x)^{j+1}} = \sum_{d = L}^{j L} \Bigl([x^d] x^L D_1(x)^{j-1}\Bigr) \binom{n - d + j}{j} \sigma^{n - d}!}$$
Notice that $x^L D_1(x)^{j-1}$ is a **finite polynomial of degree at most $j L \le 3 L$**—there is **no polynomial inversion and no Bostan–Mori**!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}
1. Compute $C_P(x)$ via KMP on $P$ in $O(L)$ time, and build the degree-$L$ polynomial $D_1(x) = (1 - \sigma x)(C_P(x) - 1) + x^L$.
2. Compute $A_1(x) = x^L$ (degree $L$), $A_2(x) = x^L D_1(x)$ (degree $2L$), and $A_3(x) = x^L D_1(x)^2$ (degree $3L$, using $1$ NTT convolution of $D_1(x)$ with itself).
3. For each $j \in \{1, 2, 3\}$, evaluate $B_j(n) = \sum_{d = L}^{\min(n, jL)} [x^d] A_j(x) \cdot \binom{n - d + j}{j} \sigma^{n - d} \bmod 998244353$ in $O(jL)$ time.
4. Convert the binomial moments $B_1(n), B_2(n), B_3(n)$ into the $3$-rd power sum via Stirling numbers of the second kind ($x^3 = 6\binom{x}{3} + 6\binom{x}{2} + \binom{x}{1}$):
   $$\mathbb{E}\bigl[\operatorname{occ}_P(W)^3\bigr] = \sigma^{-n} \Bigl(6 B_3(n) + 6 B_2(n) + B_1(n)\Bigr) \pmod{998244353}.$$
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-VI-06"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 24](../chapters/ch24-goulden-jackson-moment-shift-fps.qmd) (`T-4A-03`: The $t = 1 + u$ Binomial Moment Shift for Huge $n \le 10^{18}$ · `Universal Cup` · Decoy Pair B Part 2)**.
- **Why $[u^j]F(x, 1+u)$ Is a Pure Polynomial Divided by $(1 - \sigma x)^{j+1}$**:
  Let $y = \frac{u x^L}{1 - u(C_P(x) - 1)}$. Then:
  $$F(x, 1 + u) = \frac{1}{1 - \sigma x - y} = \frac{1}{1 - \sigma x} + \sum_{r \ge 1} \frac{y^r}{(1 - \sigma x)^{r+1}} = \frac{1}{1 - \sigma x} + \sum_{r \ge 1} \frac{u^r x^{rL}}{(1 - \sigma x)^{r+1} \bigl(1 - u(C_P(x) - 1)\bigr)^r}.$$
  Extracting $[u^j]$ ($j \ge 1$) from the sum over $1 \le r \le j$ gives:
  $$[u^j]F(x, 1 + u) = \sum_{r=1}^j \binom{j - 1}{r - 1} \frac{x^{rL} \bigl(C_P(x) - 1\bigr)^{j - r}}{(1 - \sigma x)^{r+1}} = \frac{x^L}{(1 - \sigma x)^{j+1}} \sum_{r=1}^j \binom{j - 1}{r - 1} \bigl(x^L\bigr)^{r-1} \Bigl((1 - \sigma x)\bigl(C_P(x) - 1\bigr)\Bigr)^{j - r} = \frac{x^L \, D_1(x)^{j-1}}{(1 - \sigma x)^{j+1}}!$$
  By the binomial theorem, the sum over $r = 1 \dots j$ collapses into the **polynomial power** $D_1(x)^{j-1}$!
- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-6-06`)**:
  - **Reducing $n \bmod 998244353$ Inside the Exponent $\sigma^{n - d}$**: By Fermat's Little Theorem, $\binom{n - d + j}{j}$ uses $(n - d + j) \bmod 998244353$, whereas the power $\sigma^{n - d} \bmod 998244353$ requires reducing the exponent modulo $\varphi(998244353) = 998244352$ (or multiplying $\sigma^{n \bmod (P-1)}$ by $(\sigma^{-1})^d \bmod P$). Also remember to restrict the sum to $d \le n$ when $n < 3L$!
- **Complexity**: $O(K L \log(KL))$ time ($K = 3$) and $O(KL)$ space, completely independent of $n \le 10^{18}$.
::::

### Problem `CP-VI-07` — Constrained Alignment Profile Census

You are given a template string $S[1..K]$ ($1 \le K \le 15$) and a forbidden pattern $P = \texttt{"ABA"}$ over the uppercase alphabet $\Sigma = \{\texttt{'A'}, \texttt{'B'}, \texttt{'C'}\}$, along with a target length $N$ ($1 \le N \le 1000$).

For each integer $c \in \{0, 1, \dots, K\}$, compute the number of strings $T \in \Sigma^N$ of length $N$ such that:

1. $T$ does **not** contain $\texttt{"ABA"}$ as a contiguous substring, **and**
2. The longest common subsequence of $S$ and $T$ has length $c$.

Output all $K + 1$ counts modulo $10^9 + 7$.

- **Constraints**: $1 \le K \le 15$, $1 \le N \le 1000$, $|\Sigma| = 3$, Time Limit $1.5\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $128\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination**: We are not evaluating $\operatorname{LCS}(S, T)$ for a single given $T$ (`Ch 23`); we are **counting how many outer strings $T \in \Sigma^N$ cause the inner LCS DP to output $c$**!
- **Diagnostic Signal**: This is the canonical **Automaton-over-Automaton (`DP套DP`, `Ch 25` `T-4A-05`)** problem coupled with **Bit-Parallel Allison–Dix LCS (`Ch 23` `T-4B-05`)**! In the inner DP $f[i][j] = \operatorname{LCS}(S[1..j], T[1..i])$, adjacent horizontal entries satisfy $\Delta_j = f[i][j] - f[i][j-1] \in \{0, 1\}$. Therefore, the entire inner DP row $f[i][0..K]$ is bijectively encoded as a **$K$-bit integer mask $V \in [0, 2^K)$** whose popcount $\operatorname{popcount}(V)$ equals $\operatorname{LCS}(S, T[1..i])$!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
Combine **Stage 1 of the `DP套DP` Compiler (`Ch 25`)** with the **Allison–Dix 4-Instruction Borrow Formula (`Ch 23` Theorem 23.1)**:

1. Precompute the pattern character mask $M[a] = \sum_{j=1}^K \mathbf{1}[S[j] == a] \cdot 2^{j-1}$ for each $a \in \{\texttt{'A'}, \texttt{'B'}, \texttt{'C'}\}$.
2. For any inner LCS difference mask $V \in [0, 2^K)$ and next character $a \in \Sigma$, the next LCS difference mask $V' = \operatorname{trans}_{\text{LCS}}(V, a)$ is given in **$O(1)$ time (4 bitwise operations)** without ever unpacking $V$ into an array:
   $$X = V \mathbin{|} M[a], \qquad Y = \bigl((V \ll 1) \mathbin{|} 1\bigr) \mathbin{\&} \bigl((1 \ll K) - 1\bigr), \qquad V' = X \mathbin{\&} \sim(X - Y) \mathbin{\&} \bigl((1 \ll K) - 1\bigr)!$$
3. Simultaneously track the 3-state KMP automaton $q \in \{0: \varepsilon, 1: \texttt{"A"}, 2: \texttt{"AB"}\}$ for the forbidden substring $\texttt{"ABA"}$ (where transition $(q = 2, \texttt{'A'})$ is forbidden!).
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}
1. Precompute `nxt_mask[V][a]` for all $V \in [0, 2^K)$ and $a \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ in $O(3 \cdot 2^K)$ time using the 4-instruction formula above, and hardcode the $3 \times 3$ KMP transition table `nxt_kmp[q][a]`.
2. Allocate a **rolling outer DP array** `dp[2][1 << K][3]` (to stay well inside the $128\text{ MB}$ memory limit!), initialized with `dp[0][0][0] = 1`.
3. For step $i = 1, \dots, N$, transition from `dp[(i-1)&1][V][q]` to `dp[i&1][nxt_mask[V][a]][nxt_kmp[q][a]]` whenever `nxt_kmp[q][a] < 3`.
4. After step $N$, accumulate `dp[N&1][V][q]` into `ans[__builtin_popcount(V)]` for all $V \in [0, 2^K)$ and $q \in \{0, 1, 2\}$.
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-VI-07"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 25](../chapters/ch25-martingale-pgfs-automaton-dp-of-dp.qmd) & [Chapter 23](../chapters/ch23-bit-parallel-lcs-seaweed-matrices.qmd) (`T-4A-05` + `T-4B-05`: Product `DP套DP` Compiler with Allison–Dix 4-Instruction Bit-Parallel Inner Step)**.
- **Why Allison–Dix Eliminates the $O(K \cdot 2^K)$ Inner Unpacking Loop**:
  In traditional `DP套DP` implementations (`[TJOI2018] 游园会`), contestants unpack each mask $V \in [0, 2^K)$ into prefix sums $f[0..K]$, run a length-$K$ DP loop to compute $f'[0..K]$, and re-pack $\Delta f'[j] = f'[j] - f'[j-1]$ into $V'$. By `Ch 23` Theorem 23.1, hardware subtraction $X - Y$ ($X = V \mid M[a], Y = (V \ll 1) \mid 1$) propagates borrows across each interval $(j_{r-1}, j_r]$ of 0-bits of $V$ and gets absorbed at the earliest match of $a$ in $(j_{r-1}, j_r]$, computing `nxt_mask[V][a]` in $4$ CPU instructions!
- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-6-07`)**:
  - **Forgetting to Mask $V'$ with `(1 << K) - 1`**: When the MSB (bit $K - 1$) of $V$ is $1$, $(V \ll 1) \mid 1$ sets bit $K$ in $Y$. Masking $X \mathbin{\&} \sim(X - Y)$ with `(1 << K) - 1` ensures bit $K$ never leaks into $V'$.
  - **KMP Fallback Bug on $(q = 1, \texttt{'A'})$**: When the KMP state for $\texttt{"ABA"}$ is $q = 1$ ($\texttt{"A"}$) and another $\texttt{'A'}$ arrives, the longest proper prefix of $\texttt{"AA"}$ that is a prefix of $\texttt{"ABA"}$ has length **$1$** ($q' = 1$, not $0$!).
- **Complexity**: $O((2^K + N \cdot 2^K) |\Sigma|)$ time and $O(2^K |\Sigma|)$ space.
::::

### Problem `CP-VI-08` — Non-Adjacent Subsequence Spectrum

You are given a string $S[1..N]$ over the first $\sigma$ lowercase English letters ($1 \le \sigma \le 10$, $1 \le N \le 10^5$) and $Q$ range queries ($1 \le Q \le 10^5$). Each query specifies a substring $S[l..r]$ ($1 \le l \le r \le N$) and asks for the number of **distinct non-empty strings** $W$ that can be formed by selecting a sequence of **non-adjacent indices** inside $[l, r]$:
$$l \le i_1 < i_2 < \dots < i_m \le r \quad \text{such that} \quad i_{t+1} - i_t \ge 2 \;\;\forall\, 1 \le t < m,$$
and concatenating $S[i_1] S[i_2] \cdots S[i_m]$, modulo $10^9 + 7$.

- **Constraints**: $1 \le N, Q \le 10^5$, $1 \le \sigma \le 10$, Time Limit $2.5\text{ s}$, Memory Limit $256\text{ MB}$.

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 1 — Diagnostic Signal & Decoy Elimination"}
- **Decoy Elimination (`CP-VI-08` vs. `CP-VI-01`)**: Look at how similar this is to `CP-VI-01`: we again count distinct subsequences of $S[l..r]$ modulo $10^9 + 7$, except chosen indices must satisfy the **gap-$2$ condition $i_{t+1} - i_t \ge 2$**! Why does `CP-VI-01`'s $O((N+Q)\sigma)$ prefix-matrix inversion **fail** here?
- **Diagnostic Signal**: In the gap-$2$ automaton $\text{DASG}_{\text{gap}=2}(S)$, an index $i$ can only extend a canonical prefix ending at $j \le i - 2$. When character $c = S[i]$ is processed in a buffered DP state $(f_1, \dots, f_\sigma, b_1, \dots, b_\sigma)$ where the buffer $b_c$ overwrites $f_c$ from two steps ago without adding the current $f_c$, the single-step transition matrix has **determinant $\det M_c = 0$ (singular)**!
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 2 — Combinatorial Word Invariant"}
1. **Leftmost Gap-2 Canonicalization (`ABC 214F`)**:
   By the exchange argument (`Ch 22` Theorem 22.1 & `§3.2.2`), a string $W = c_1 \dots c_m$ has a gap-2 embedding in $S[l..r]$ iff its **leftmost gap-2 greedy embedding** finishes at $\le r$:
   - From the virtual root $l - 1$ ($\varepsilon$), the first character $c_1$ matches at $i_1 = \operatorname{nxt}[l - 1][c_1] \in \{l, l + 1, \dots, r\}$ (gap $\ge 1$ from $l - 1$, so **both $i_1 = l$ and $i_1 = l + 1$ are reachable from the root**!).
   - From any real index $i_{t-1} \ge l$, the next character $c_t$ ($t \ge 2$) matches at $i_t = \operatorname{nxt}[i_{t-1} + 1][c_t]$ (enforcing $i_t \ge i_{t-1} + 2$).
2. **Exact Whole-String Pull Recurrence ($l = 1$)**:
   Let $dp[i]$ be the number of canonical gap-2 paths ending at index $i$ (with $dp[0] = 1$ for $\varepsilon$ and $dp[1] = 1$ for $S[1]$). For $i \ge 2$, let $p = \operatorname{prev}[i] < i$ be the previous occurrence of $S[i]$. Which earlier states $j \le i - 2$ were **not** already extended by $S[p] = S[i]$ at step $p$?
   - If $p = 0$ (first occurrence of $S[i]$): no $j$ was extended yet, so $j \in [0, i - 2]$.
   - If $p = 1$: step $p = 1$ already extended the virtual root $j = 0$, so $j \in [1, i - 2]$.
   - If $p \ge 2$: step $p$ only extended $j \le p - 2$, leaving **$j = p - 1$ unextended**, so $j \in [p - 1, i - 2]$!
   $$\boxed{dp[i] = \sum_{j = L(i)}^{i - 2} dp[j] \quad (i \ge 2), \qquad L(i) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{if } \operatorname{prev}[i] = 0, \\ 1 & \text{if } \operatorname{prev}[i] = 1, \\ \operatorname{prev}[i] - 1 & \text{if } \operatorname{prev}[i] \ge 2. \end{cases}}$$
::::

:::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Hint 3 — Algorithmic & Data-Structure Assembly"}
To answer $Q$ range queries $[l, r]$ ($1 \le N, Q \le 10^5, \sigma \le 10$):

1. Observe that in $\text{DASG}_{\text{gap}=2}(S)$, any path inside $[l, r]$ is a directed path where each node $u$ transitions to $\operatorname{nxt}[u + 1][c]$ for $c \in \Sigma$ (and the root $l - 1$ transitions to $\operatorname{nxt}[l - 1][c]$).
2. Use **Offline Divide-and-Conquer over $[L, R]$** (or a Segment Tree of $(\sigma + 1) \times (\sigma + 1)$ transfer matrices over consecutive index pairs):
   - For a midpoint $M = \lfloor(L + R)/2\rfloor$, any valid gap-2 subsequence of $S[l..r]$ ($l \le M < r$) either lies wholly in $[l, M]$, wholly in $[M + 1, r]$, or jumps across the cut from a last index $u \le M$ to a first index $v = \operatorname{nxt}[\max(l - 1, u + 1)][c] \ge M + 1$.
   - Notice that every cross-cut jump $u \to v$ lands on one of at most **$2\sigma$ entry positions** in $[M + 1, R]$: either $\operatorname{nxt}[M][c]$ (from $u \le M - 1$) or $\operatorname{nxt}[M + 1][c]$ (from $u = M$)!
   - Running the $O(R - M)$ forward recurrence from those $\le 2\sigma$ right-half entry states and the $O(M - L)$ backward recurrence on $[L, M]$ answers each cross-midpoint query $[l, r]$ in $O(\sigma)$ time!
::::

:::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Complete Derivation, Complexity Proof & Reference Solution — CP-VI-08"}

- **Target Chapter & Technique ID**: **[Chapter 22](../chapters/ch22-dasg-arch-simon-invertible-matrices.qmd) (`T-4B-03` Singular $\det = 0$ Counterexample: Gap-2 Distinct Subsequences via $\text{DASG}_{\text{gap}=2}$ Divide-and-Conquer)**.
- **Hand-Checkable Verification of the Lower Bound $L(i)$**:
  1. $S = \texttt{"aa"}$ ($N = 2$): $dp[0] = 1, dp[1] = 1$ ($\texttt{"a"}$). At $i = 2$, $\operatorname{prev}[2] = 1 \implies L(2) = 1 > 2 - 2 = 0 \implies dp[2] = 0$. Total $= dp[1] + dp[2] = 1$ ($\{\texttt{"a"}\}$).
  2. $S = \texttt{"acaa"}$ ($N = 4$): $dp[0] = 1, dp[1] = 1$ ($\texttt{"a"}$), $dp[2] = 1$ ($\texttt{"c"}$). At $i = 3$ ($\texttt{'a'}$), $\operatorname{prev}[3] = 1 \implies L(3) = 1 \implies dp[3] = dp[1] = 1$ ($\texttt{"aa"}$). At $i = 4$ ($\texttt{'a'}$), $\operatorname{prev}[4] = 3 \ge 2 \implies L(4) = 3 - 1 = 2 \implies dp[4] = dp[2] = 1$ ($\texttt{"ca"}$, since index $3$ was adjacent to index $2$ and could not extend $\texttt{"c"}$, whereas index $4$ is at distance $2$ from index $2$!). Total $= 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 4$ ($\{\texttt{"a"}, \texttt{"c"}, \texttt{"aa"}, \texttt{"ca"}\}$).
- **Boundary Pitfall Audit (`BP-6-08`)**:
  - **Using $L(i) = \operatorname{prev}[i] - 1 = 0$ When $\operatorname{prev}[i] = 1$**: Because the virtual root $j = 0$ transitions to $i_1 = 1$ with gap $1$ whereas real indices require gap $\ge 2$, an occurrence at $p = 1$ already consumes $j = 0$. Setting $L(i) = 0$ when $\operatorname{prev}[i] = 1$ double-counts the single-character string $S[1]$ at the second occurrence of $S[1]$.
- **Complexity**: $O(N)$ for whole-string counting (`ABC 214F`); $O((N \sigma + Q)\sigma \log N)$ for range queries $[l, r]$.
::::

::::
